Research Brief IPCid : The Single registry: two popular sayings and the names of things
results.abstract: The document analyzes the recent trajectory of Brazil’s Single Registry (CadÚnico), highlighting its state of obsolescence until 2022 and the negative impacts of the Auxílio Brasil program on the composition of beneficiaries. It presents the corrective actions implemented since 2023, including the review of records, data integration with CNIS and the Presença System, removal of inconsistent registrations, and the reinstatement of the Bolsa Família program. It also emphasizes modernization initiatives, capacity building for managers, the creation of the Single Registry Observatory, and the importance of treating the system as a central tool for social inclusion, avoiding stigmatization of vulnerable families.

results.title: A Comprehensive Practice Package to Support Clinical Competence and Transition of Newly Qualified Registered Nurses
results.abstract: Background: Transitioning from nursing education to independent clinical practice is a critical and often challenging period for newly qualified registered nurses (NQRNs). During this phase, NQRNs frequently face high workloads, limited mentorship, stress, and gaps in clinical competence, which can affect both patient care and nurse retention. Structured support systems are therefore essential to foster competence, resilience, and professional growth. Aim: This study explored transition challenges of NQRNs and proposed a structured competency package to enhance clinical practice and professional development. Methods: A sequential explanatory mixed-methods design was used. In the quantitative phase, 272 NQRNs from Chris Hani District completed a survey on training, mentorship, workload, stress, continuing education, and leadership. In the qualitative phase, 25 purposively selected participants joined three focus group discussions exploring lived experiences and support needs. Data were analysed using SPSS for descriptive and inferential statistics and Braun and Clarke’s six-phase thematic framework, with ethical approval and trustworthiness ensured through standard qualitative rigor. Results: Findings indicated that many NQRNs experienced only moderate satisfaction with their transition support, high stress levels, and feelings of being overwhelmed by workload. Mentorship effectiveness was perceived as inconsistent, whereas the importance of continuing education and professional development was rated highly. Conclusions: The study informed a structured, stage-based competency package combining skills training, mentorship, critical thinking, communication, ethical practice, resilience support, and continuous assessment. This holistic framework aims to enhance clinical competence, confidence, and adaptive capacity among NQRNs, supporting safe, patient-centred care and long-term workforce retention.

results.title: Causal Engram Circuits for Factual and Hallucinated Memory in Large Language Models
results.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) produce fluent yet factually incorrect statements—a failure that mirrors false memory in biological systems. Whether such errors arise from causally identifiable and manipulable circuit elements has remained unknown. Here we adapt the engram framework from systems neuroscience and combine causal mediation analysis with a double-dissociation logic to localize, verify, and rewrite factual and false memory traces in GPT-style transformers. We discover that sparse sets of knowledge neurons—canonical ensembles of approximately 8–15 units—function as memory engrams: silencing them selectively erases target-fact retrieval while matched controls remain intact; exogenous activation forces the fact into output even under neutral prompts. Rigorous controls, including patterned activation and non-engram amplification, confirm identity-specific sufficiency. Critically, counterfactual fine-tuning creates false memory engrams that deviate geometrically toward lexical co-occurrence subspaces; formal mediation analysis reveals that this geometric corruption causally mediates 65% of the pathway from falsity to erroneous output. Exploiting this divergence, we construct an unsupervised Memory Credibility Score that predicts hallucination propensity without behavioural testing, generalizing across relations and model scales. The framework extends to multi-hop and temporal reasoning and enables reversible, context-dependent memory control unavailable to permanent weight-editing methods. Our findings establish a causal sufficiency-and-necessity account of factual retrieval, diagnose representational pathologies underlying hallucination, and deliver a precision toolkit for understanding and certifying knowledge in LLMs.

Hallucinated Authority: AI Citations as Reckless Misrepresentation
results.abstract:
When courts sanctioned the attorneys in Mata v. Avianca for submitting AI-generated citations to nonexistent cases, they reached for the vocabulary of negligence. That characterization is wrong. Large language models do not forget cases the way attorneys do; they generate citations that look real but correspond to nothing in any reporter, and they do so at documented rates of 58% to 88% on legal queries, a fact publicly known in peer-reviewed research before most of the incidents now filling the reporters. An attorney who submits AI output without verification does not merely fail a diligence standard. She submits a representation to a court while consciously declining to establish any basis for its accuracy, satisfying the elements of reckless misrepresentation under Restatement (Second) of Torts § 526(b)–(c). The cases that have followed Mata reach instinctively for language that exceeds negligence, calling citations “bogus” and monetary sanctions “insufficient deterrents,” and some have begun to reach the word “reckless” without grounding that intuition in a cross-regime doctrinal framework. This Article supplies that framework.

This Article makes three original contributions. First, it introduces the concept of “structurally predictable error” to explain why AI hallucination is categorically different from human memory failure: the error follows from the tool's architecture rather than from individual cognitive lapse, its rate is publicly documented, and a reasonable practitioner in the field either knows or should know it before using the tool. Second, it builds the doctrinal case for reckless misrepresentation by connecting § 526(b)–(c) to the philosophy of AI output, arguing that an attorney who relies on a tool architecturally indifferent to the distinction between true and false adopts that indifference as her own representational posture toward the court. Third, it proposes a graduated three-tier accountability framework that calibrates sanctions to actual culpability, preserving space for good-faith verification efforts and the access-to-justice benefits that AI tools offer to under-resourced practitioners, while refusing to treat willful blindness toward a known category of fabrication as mere carelessness.

results.title: Hallucinated Legal Presentations in Civil Trial Courts
results.abstract:
Increasingly hallucinated legal presentations are being discovered and sanctioned in U.S. federal and state civil trial courts.  Such presentations encompass papers that are signed, filed, submitted or advocated which contain nonexistent legal sources, whether case precedents, statutes, court rules, administrative regulations, or otherwise.  These presentations may be discovered by judges, presenting lawyers, opposing lawyers, unrepresented parties, or witnesses.  Sanctions may follow under court rules, like Federal Civil Procedure Rule (FRCP) 11 and its state court rule counterparts, federal or state statutes, or both.

Discoveries and sanctions are most often facilitated by FRCP 11 and similar state court rules of general application.  They are less easily undertaken by state court rules or statutes that only partially follow, or significantly differ from, FRCP 11.  This essay demonstrates the enhanced FRCP 11 opportunities for early and easy discovery and sanction of hallucinated legal presentations, as well as the difficulties posed when FRCP 11 is not (fully) followed in state trial courts.

The essay employs the 2025 Minnesota State District Court opinion in Nuvola, LLC v. Morgan Wright to address the current deficient norms on hallucinated legal presentations.  In Minnesota, state lawmakers have only partially follow FRCP 11.  The case is examined under FRCP 11 and comparable state civil procedure laws.  Some state laws differ significantly from both the federal and Minnesota laws.  The essay highlights the greater breadth of FRCP 11 in addressing troublesome paper presentations, the rule’s safe harbor provisions, and the rule’s recognition of law firm responsibility for frivolous presentations.  The essay includes suggestions on how trial court norms can better address hallucinated legal presentations by lawyers.  In doing so, it may also assist lawmakers contemplating civil procedure law reforms addressing hallucinated facts, like deepfakes, and hallucinated opinions, as from alleged experts.

Persistence Hallucinated? Research Integrity Issues in Voigtländer and Voth (2012)
results.abstract: Voigtländer and Voth's (2012) study of the medieval origins of antisemitic violence in Nazi Germany has various research integrity issues. Their research design is supposed to rely on "unambiguous information" that often does not exist in their sources. Furthermore, when such information does exist, it frequently contradicts the dataset that is supposed to have been coded from those sources. There are also unexplained discrepancies in their dataset relating to the official statistics of the deportations of Germany's Jews during the Holocaust. As a result, Voigtländer and Voth's (2012) study cannot be replicated.

The End-of-Day Reversal After 2019: A Pre-Registered Test on S&P 500 Stocks Excluding Heavily Traded Names
results.abstract: Baltussen, Da and Soebhag (2025) document an end-of-day reversal in U.S. stocks through December 2019: intraday losers outperform intraday winners over the last half hour of trading. We test it on later data, on point-in-time S&P 500 members excluding about 80 heavily traded stocks we had examined in earlier, unpublished work. Under a private pre-registration, the 2016–2019 data had to reproduce the published sign before any statistic linking the sort to the outcome was computed on later primary-sample data. Measured to the last trade before the closing auction, the dollar-volume-weighted reversal is 3.13 bps per day (t = 7.5) in 2016–2019 and 3.05 bps (t = 3.0) in 2023–2026, with a one-sided 95% bound on the decline of 61%. The result depends on the window: the reversal is indistinguishable from zero in 2020–2022, 2023 carries much of the later estimate, and from 2020 onward it is 1.69 bps (t = 2.3), with a bound of 91%. A proxy sample, added after the run, gives 2.81 and 3.86 bps. On the full index the reversal falls from 3.40 to 0.74 bps (t of the change −1.83, short of the registered bar of −3); descriptive comparisons concentrate this weakness in the very largest stocks. No pre-registered mechanism test passes.
